usecases.title: Automated booking abuse (slot scalping bots)
usecases.attack: T1499.003 Application Exhaustion Flood

rules.description: UC01 Booking bot: account $(username) made 10+ booking attempts in 60 seconds from $(srcip).
UC01 Booking bot farm: 15+ booking attempts in 60 seconds from $(srcip) using rotating accounts.

say.why: Arrival slots sell out in minutes; bots grab them for resale, so real pilgrims lose their place.
say.logic: Silent base rule counts booking attempts; 10 per account per minute, or 15 per IP across rotating accounts, alerts.
say.fp: Shared hotel and carrier NAT gets a higher per-IP threshold; load-test IPs are a CDB list; ignore=120 stops alert storms.
say.improve: Active response to block the IP for 10 minutes on the bot-farm rule.

usecases.why_long: Hajj and Umrah arrival slots are scarce and sell out in minutes. Bots grab them for resale on the black market, so genuine pilgrims lose their place and fake 'guaranteed package' sellers get stock. No input validation stops this: each request is a perfectly valid booking. Only behaviour gives it away.
logic: Base rule 110013 (level 2) tags every `booking_attempt`. It is not shown as an alert but is counted.
110101: the same `username` makes 10 attempts within 60 s (`frequency=10`, `same_field username`). A person manages 1-3 a minute through the UI.
110102: 15 attempts from one `srcip` within 60 s, using rotating accounts (`same_srcip`, `different_field username`). This is a bot farm spreading load across stolen or fake accounts.
fp: Thousands of pilgrims share hotel and carrier NAT addresses during the season, so the per-IP rule needs a higher threshold than the per-account rule.
Known shared or test IPs (campaign offices, load-test agents) go in `etc/lists/pp-trusted-ips` and are skipped.
`ignore="120"`: once a bot is flagged, the rule stays quiet for 2 minutes instead of firing every 10 requests.
improve: Add active response (`firewall-drop` on `srcip`, 10 min) for 110102.
Feed CAPTCHA or bot-score results into the audit log and correlate with them.
Baseline per-season booking rates and adapt the thresholds for opening day.

cases.title: One account fires 10 booking attempts in a minute -> 110101
15 attempts from one IP, rotating accounts -> 110102
9 attempts stays under the threshold (no alert)
Load-test agent on the trusted list is ignored

test: Sign in as `pilgrim0042` / `Pilgrim#2026` and open **Bookings**.
Click **Book** on 10 different slots within a minute (results like *full* or *duplicate* still count).
In Wazuh, filter `rule.id:110101`. The alert names the account and source IP.

usecases.title: Credential stuffing and password guessing
usecases.attack: T1110.004 Credential Stuffing, T1110.001 Password Guessing

rules.description: UC02 Possible credential stuffing: failed logins for 8+ different accounts from $(srcip) in 2 minutes.
UC02 Credential stuffing: $(srcip) tried 5+ non-existent accounts in 2 minutes (leaked combo list pattern).
UC02 Password guessing: 6+ wrong passwords for account $(username) in 2 minutes (latest from $(srcip)).

say.why: One stolen agency login exposes thousands of pilgrims' passports and bookings.
say.logic: Failures are split by reason; non-existent usernames from one IP (110202) is the high-confidence stuffing signal.
say.fp: Hotel NAT mistypes stay below thresholds; the scanner is allowlisted; duplicate nginx 401 alerts are absorbed by a no_log tuning rule.
say.improve: Enrich the source IP with a threat-intel CDB list of proxy and botnet ranges.

usecases.why_long: Leaked email/password lists are replayed against every big portal. A hijacked pilgrim account exposes a passport and payments; a hijacked agency account exposes thousands of pilgrims and their bookings.
logic: The base rules split failures by reason: 110011 is a wrong password for a real account (`pp_bad_password`), 110012 is a non-existent account (`pp_unknown_user`).
110201 (level 8): 8 failures from one IP for 8 different accounts in 2 min.

110202 (level 11): 5 attempts for non-existent accounts from one IP in 2 min. Combo lists are full of accounts the portal never had; real users almost never mistype a username into a non-existent account.
110203 (level 10): 6 wrong passwords for one account in 2 min, from any IP (password guessing).
All three carry group `pp_bruteforce`, which UC03 correlates with a later success.
fp: Hotel and carrier NAT: several genuine pilgrims mistyping passwords from one IP is normal, so 110201 stays at medium and the high-confidence signal is 110202.
The internal vulnerability scanner and load-test agents are allowlisted in `pp-trusted-ips`.
Thresholds sit just above normal behaviour (a person retries 2-3 times) and are documented here for tuning.

Duplicate suppression: nginx logs each failed sign-in as HTTP 401, which would also raise Wazuh's generic 'Web server 400 error code' (31101). Tuning rule 110021 absorbs exactly those lines with `no_log`, so the dashboard shows the UC02 alert only (regression cases UC02-06 and UC02-07).
improve: Active response on 110202 to block the IP for 15 minutes.
Enrich `srcip` with a threat-intelligence CDB list of known proxy and botnet ranges.
Track the ratio of failures to successes per IP over an hour (SIEM dashboard).

5 non-existent accounts from one IP -> 110202 (high confidence)
6 wrong passwords for one agency account -> 110203

Internal scanner on the trusted list is ignored
Tuning: nginx 401 for a failed sign-in is absorbed (no duplicate 31101 alert)
Tuning keeps other 4xx: a scanner probing /wp-admin still raises 31101

Enter wrong passwords for `pilgrim0001` to `pilgrim0008`, which gives 110201.
Enter a wrong password for `agency.in01` 6 times, which gives 110203.

usecases.title: Account takeover after a credential attack
usecases.attack: T1110 Brute Force then T1078 Valid Accounts

rules.description: UC03 Account takeover suspected: $(username) logged in from $(srcip) right after a credential attack from the same IP.
UC03 Account takeover suspected: $(username) logged in (from $(srcip)) shortly after a password-guessing attack on that account.

say.why: A failed attack is noise; a failed attack followed by a success is a compromised account.
say.logic: A successful login correlated with a brute-force alert from the same IP, or on the same account, within 10 minutes.
say.fp: Both halves are required and tied by IP or username; an unrelated login after an attack does not fire.
say.improve: Chain takeover with a later bulk export or price override for a level-15 alert.

usecases.why_long: A failed attack is noise; a failed attack followed by a success is a compromised account. That is the moment the SOC must act: reset the password, kill the session and review what was booked or exported.
logic: 110301: a `login_success` from an IP that raised any `pp_bruteforce` alert in the last 10 min (`if_sid 110010` + `if_matched_group pp_bruteforce` + `same_srcip`).
110302: a `login_success` for an account that was the target of password guessing (group `pp_password_guessing`) in the last 10 min, even if the attacker switched IP (`same_field username`).
Both are level 13 and also carry `pp_login_success`, so UC04 still counts these logins.
fp: The correlation needs both halves, the attack and a success tied by IP or account, within 10 minutes.
A different user signing in from a different IP after an attack does not fire (regression case UC03-03).
improve: Active response: disable the account or revoke sessions through the portal API.
Add a third correlation: takeover followed by a bulk export or price override (UC09/UC08) to reach level 15.

Password guessing on an account, attacker switches IP, then success -> 110302
Unrelated user logs in from another IP after an attack (no takeover alert)

test: From your laptop, trigger 110202 (5 made-up usernames, see UC02).
Then sign in correctly as `pilgrim0007` / `Pilgrim#2026` from the same laptop, which gives 110301.
Or: 6 wrong passwords for `agency.in01`, then the right one (`Agency#2026`), which gives 110302.

usecases.title: Impossible travel
usecases.attack: T1078 Valid Accounts

rules.description: UC04 Impossible travel: $(username) logged in from $(country) ($(srcip)) less than an hour after a login from another country.

say.why: Pilgrims log in from everywhere, so 'abroad' means nothing; two countries in an hour on one account does.
say.logic: Two successful logins for the same account from different countries within one hour (GeoIP on the source IP).
say.fp: Corporate VPN egress IPs are a CDB list; the rule needs two successes, not failures.
say.improve: Add device fingerprint and ASN to tell a travelling pilgrim from a proxy.

usecases.why_long: Pilgrims and agencies log in from every country, so 'login from abroad' means nothing here. Two countries within one hour on the same account does: the password is being used by someone else, usually through a proxy or a stolen session.
logic: The portal resolves the client IP to a country (DB-IP Lite database, ip-api.com fallback) and logs it on every login.

110401: two successful logins for the same `username` from different `country` values within 3600 s (`frequency=2`, `same_field username`, `different_field country`, counted through group `pp_login_success`).
fp: A pilgrim in India in the morning and in Jeddah six hours later does not fire: that is a flight, outside the 1-hour window.
Corporate and campaign VPN exit IPs are skipped through `etc/lists/pp-vpn-egress`.
Known limitation: neighbouring countries (e.g. SA-BH over the causeway) cannot be expressed as a pair in a Wazuh 4.x rule.
improve: Have the portal compute travel speed between consecutive logins (km/h) and alert above about 900 km/h, which also handles neighbouring countries.
Add ASN/hosting-provider enrichment to flag VPS and Tor exits.

usecases.title: Pilgrim record harvesting and authorization probing
usecases.attack: T1213 Data from Information Repositories; T1190 (probing access control)

rules.description: UC05 Record harvesting: $(username) [$(role)] opened 12+ different pilgrim records in 3 minutes.
UC05 Authorization probing: $(username) [$(role)] was denied 5+ pilgrim records in 2 minutes (IDOR attempt).

say.why: Staff accounts can open any pilgrim record; harvesting them is how passport data leaks.
say.logic: 12 different records in 3 minutes by one account, or 5 denied record lookups (IDOR probing).
say.fp: Visa reviewers who legitimately page through records are a CDB list.
say.improve: Per-role baselines: an agency should only ever open its own pilgrims.

usecases.why_long: Pilgrim records hold passport numbers and phone numbers, which are prime material for visa fraud and fake-Hajj scams. The biggest risk is an authorised insider quietly collecting records, and access control cannot stop someone who is allowed in.
logic: 110501: the same account opens 12 *different* records in 3 minutes (`different_field pilgrim_id`). Re-opening one record does not count. A case handler works 3-5 records in that time.
110502: the same account is denied 5 records in 2 minutes. Someone is walking record IDs that are not theirs (an IDOR attempt); the portal blocks it and the SIEM reports it.
fp: Approved bulk reviewers (e.g. during visa-processing peaks) are listed in `etc/lists/pp-bulk-reviewers`.
Duplicate suppression: tuning rule 110022 absorbs the nginx 403/404 lines for refused record requests, which would otherwise raise the generic 31101 alert next to UC05 (regression case UC05-05).
`ignore="300"` avoids repeat alerts while one investigation is open.
improve: Weight sensitive views (passport shown in full) higher than list views.
Correlate harvesting with a following export (UC09) as a level-15 data-theft chain.

Tuning: nginx 403 for a refused record is absorbed (no duplicate 31101 alert)

Sign in as `pilgrim0042`, then type `/records/1100`, `/records/1101` ... `/records/1104` in the address bar. Each returns 403 and the fifth fires 110502.

usecases.title: SQL injection attempts (edge and application)
usecases.attack: T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application

rules.description: UC06 SQL injection attempt against the portal from $(srcip): $(url)
UC06 Automated SQL injection scanning: 5+ injection attempts from $(srcip) in 60 seconds.
UC06 SQL injection attempt in the permit search parameter from $(srcip) (decoded at the application).
UC06 SQL injection from $(srcip) seen at the edge AND reaching the application search handler.
UC06 Automated SQL injection reaching the application: 5+ injection searches from $(srcip) in 60 seconds.

say.why: The permit search is public-facing; SQL injection there would expose the whole booking database.
say.logic: Edge (nginx URL) and application (search field) detections, correlated when both see the same source within 30 s.
say.fp: Grammar-based patterns (UNION SELECT, OR 1=1, time functions), not keywords: a search for O'Brien or the word 'union' does not fire (case UC06-05).
say.improve: Active response to block the IP after the edge burst rule.

usecases.why_long: The public permit-status search is the portal's most exposed input. The portal uses parameterised queries, so injection fails, but every attempt is reconnaissance by someone targeting pilgrim data, and scanners hammer such pages during the season.
logic: 110601 (edge): injection grammar in the URL, including URL-encoded forms: quote-plus-boolean tautologies, `UNION SELECT`, comment terminators after a quote, time-based functions, schema tables, stacked queries.
110602: 5 edge attempts from one IP in 60 s indicates an automated scanner.
110603 (application): the same grammar in the decoded `q` field, with no encoding tricks to hide behind.
110604: the injection was seen at the edge AND reached the application handler from the same IP within 30 s.

Why not the built-in 31103: it matches a few literal strings and, on HTTP 200, ends as 31106 'attack returned 200 (success)', which is misleading for a parameterised app that simply answered 'no results'. Wazuh tries sibling rules highest level first, so these rules take precedence.
fp: The patterns require injection *structure*, not keywords: 'Abdullah D'Or' or 'Union Travel' do not match (regression case UC06-05).
Approved internal scanners are allowlisted in `pp-trusted-ips`.
improve: Active response to block the IP on 110602.
Add a WAF (ModSecurity CRS) and ingest its audit log for a third detection layer.

UNION SELECT and time-based probes, 5 in a row from one IP -> 110602
Injection grammar in the decoded search parameter -> 110603
Same request seen by the app and then the edge -> 110604
Legitimate searches with an apostrophe or the word union (no alert)
Found live: 5 injection searches seen by app then edge -> burst 110605

test: Open **Permit status** and search for `x' OR 'a'='a`.
The portal answers 'No permit found' (parameterised query). Wazuh shows 110603 then 110604.

Wait 30 seconds. In the browser's address bar open `http://<web01-ip>/?q=x' UNION SELECT NULL--` and press F5 four more times within a minute (5 requests in all), which gives 110602. This burst is counted at the edge only: requests that also reach the search handler become 110604 instead.

usecases.title: Web shell and web-tier compromise
usecases.attack: T1505.003 Web Shell, T1059.004 Unix Shell

rules.description: UC07 Web shell suspected: server-side script $(file) appeared in the portal web root.
UC07 Web tier executed a command: $(audit.exe) run by uid $(audit.euid) (comm: $(audit.command)).
UC07 Web shell confirmed: a script was dropped in the web root and the web tier then executed $(audit.exe).
UC07 Blocked upload of a server-side script or executable ($(filename)) by $(username) from $(srcip).

say.why: A web shell on the booking server is full control of bookings and pilgrim data.
say.logic: FIM sees a script land in the web root; auditd sees the web account run a program; together within 15 min is level 15.
say.fp: Only script extensions in the web root; programs the portal needs are a CDB allowlist; deploys never run as www-data.
say.improve: Quarantine the file automatically with active response.

usecases.why_long: A web shell gives an attacker a permanent foothold on the server that holds every pilgrim's data, and is the usual first step of ransomware and data theft against public portals.
logic: 110704 (early warning): the portal's upload allowlist rejected a server-side script or executable, for example `passport.php` posing as a scan.
110701: a script file (php, jsp, aspx, cgi, pl, py, sh ...) is created or modified in the web root. The portal is a Python app, so no executable code should ever appear there.

110702: a web service account (nginx `www-data` or the `portal` user) executes a program. Neither ever does in normal operation. auditd records it under key `pp_web_exec`; `ppid!=1` excludes systemd starting the service.
110703 (level 15): a script dropped, then the web tier executes commands within 15 minutes on the same server.
fp: FIM is scoped to the web root and to script extensions only (a CSS change does not fire, case UC07-04).
Binaries the web tier legitimately needs can be added to `etc/lists/pp-web-allowed-binaries` without editing the rule.
Deployments run as a CI user, never as `www-data`.
improve: Active response: quarantine the file (move it out of the web root) on 110701.
Hash new web-root files against a malware-hash CDB list or VirusTotal integration.

Web service account (www-data) executes a program -> 110702
Script dropped, then the web tier runs a command -> 110703 (level 15)
Static asset (CSS) change in the web root (no alert)
Upload allowlist blocks a .php disguised as a passport scan -> 110704
Wrong document type (.docx) rejected - user error, not an attack (no alert)

usecases.title: Package price override abuse (insider fraud)
usecases.attack: T1565.001 Stored Data Manipulation

rules.description: UC08 Large discount: $(username) cut $(package_id) by $(discount_pct)% ($(list_price) to $(new_price) SAR), reason: $(reason_code).
UC08 Unauthorized price override: $(username) is not a finance approver ($(package_id) set to $(new_price) SAR).
UC08 Unauthorized large discount: $(username) (not an approver) cut $(package_id) by $(discount_pct)% to $(new_price) SAR.
UC08 Repeated price overrides: $(username) made 4+ overrides in 10 minutes.

say.why: Price override is a built-in insider-fraud path: a 45,000 SAR VIP package sold for 4,500.
say.logic: Big discounts (30%+), overrides by non-approvers, both together (level 14), and 4 overrides in 10 minutes.
say.fp: Finance approvers are a CDB list owned by Finance; small goodwill discounts stay as an audit trail.
say.improve: Require a booking reference and flag overrides on the operator's own bookings.

usecases.why_long: Staff can override a package price for VIP guests or compensation. That power is a classic insider-fraud path, for example selling a 45,000 SAR VIP package to a friend for 4,500. The app allows it by design, so governance is a detective control.
logic: 110801: discount of 30% or more (regex `^(?:[3-9]\d|100)$` on `discount_pct`, since Wazuh 4.x has no numeric comparison).
110802: override by an account not on the finance approvers CDB list.
110803 (level 14): both of the above.
110804: 4 overrides by one account within 10 minutes (counted through group `pp_price_override`).
Sibling order matters: Wazuh tries the higher-level sibling first, so the non-approver path (12, then child 14) is evaluated before the plain large-discount rule (10).
fp: Approvers live in `etc/lists/pp-price-approvers`, owned by Finance, so no rule edits are needed when roles change.
Small goodwill discounts by approvers stay as the level-3 audit trail (case UC08-05).
improve: Require a `booking_ref` and correlate with the booking owner (overrides on one's own or relatives' bookings).
Weekly SIEM report of overrides per staff member for the finance controller.

Non-approver changes a price (10%) -> 110802
Non-approver gives a 90% discount -> 110803 (level 14)
Approver makes 4 small overrides in 10 minutes -> 110804
Approver gives a 10% goodwill discount (audit trail only)

usecases.title: Bulk export of pilgrim data
usecases.attack: T1213 Data from Information Repositories

rules.description: UC09 Bulk export: $(username) [$(role)] exported $(record_count) pilgrim records (scope: $(scope)).
UC09 Bulk export by a non-approved account: $(username) [$(role)] exported $(record_count) pilgrim records.
UC09 Off-hours bulk export: $(username) exported $(record_count) pilgrim records outside working hours.
UC09 Off-hours bulk export by a non-approved account: $(username) exported $(record_count) pilgrim records.

say.why: A manifest of names and passports is exactly what fake-Hajj-package scammers buy.
say.logic: 1,000+ records in one export; escalates for non-approved accounts and for off-hours (10 pm - 6 am).
say.fp: Approved exporters are a CDB list owned by the Data Protection Officer.
say.improve: Daily cumulative-volume check for many small exports.

usecases.why_long: An exported manifest of names, passports and phones is exactly what fake-Hajj-package scammers buy. Normal exports are an agency's own few hundred pilgrims; thousands at once must be explained.
logic: 110901: an export of 1,000 records or more (regex `^[1-9]\d{3,}$` on `record_count`).
110902 (13): ...by an account not on `pp-approved-exporters`.
110903 (12): ...outside working hours (`<time>10 pm - 6 am</time>`).
110904 (14): non-approved and off-hours.
fp: The approved-exporters list is owned by the Data Protection Officer.
Working hours follow the manager's clock; widen the window for 24/7 operations shifts during the season.
improve: Add a daily cumulative-volume check (many small exports that add up).
Correlate with UC03 (takeover) or UC05 (harvesting) for a level-15 data-theft chain.

usecases.title: Phishing attachment runs (HTA, script, Office spawning a shell)
usecases.attack: T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment, T1204.002 Malicious File, T1218.005 Mshta

rules.description: UC10 Phishing attachment: mshta.exe opened an HTA from a mail/download location on $(win.system.computer): $(win.eventdata.commandLine)
UC10 Phishing attachment: script host ran a downloaded script on $(win.system.computer): $(win.eventdata.commandLine)
UC10 Office application started $(win.eventdata.image) on $(win.system.computer) (parent $(win.eventdata.parentImage)) - malicious document likely.

say.why: Staff live in their inbox in season; one click on a fake visa or Nusuk invoice is the usual first step.
say.logic: mshta or a script host running from Downloads/Temp/Outlook cache, or Office starting a shell.
say.fp: Scope is user-download locations only; IT logon scripts run from netlogon or Program Files.
say.improve: Send the attachment hash to the VirusTotal integration already on the manager.

usecases.why_long: Agency and back-office staff live in their inbox during the season: visa updates, Nusuk invoices, permit confirmations and group rooming lists all arrive as attachments. Office now blocks internet macros, so attackers send HTA files, scripts and shortcuts instead. One click on a staff PC is the usual first step towards the booking systems and the passport share.
logic: 111001: `mshta.exe` opens an HTA from Downloads, Temp, the browser cache or the Outlook cache, or straight from a URL.
111002: `wscript`/`cscript` runs a `.js/.jse/.vbs/.vbe/.wsf` file from those same download locations.
111003: Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook or OneNote starts a shell, script host or LOLBin (`cmd`, `powershell`, `mshta`, `rundll32`, `certutil`...).

Every process rule hangs under 61603 and under Wazuh's level-0 classifiers 92025/92028/92042/92069, because Wazuh tries level-0 rules first and they would otherwise absorb the event (engine note in the README).
fp: Only user-download locations count: IT logon scripts run from `\\server\netlogon` or Program Files.
Office starting a shell is rare in this organisation, so it is always worth a look.
Negative cases UC10-04/05 prove that an admin script from a protected folder stays quiet.
improve: Add Sysmon event 11 for files dropped by Outlook into `Content.Outlook` and correlate the drop with the execution.
Active response: kill the process tree and isolate the host with a firewall rule.
Send the attachment hash to the VirusTotal integration that is already configured on the manager.

usecases.title: Obfuscated PowerShell and download cradles
usecases.attack: T1059.001 PowerShell, T1027 Obfuscated Files, T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer

rules.description: UC11 Obfuscated PowerShell on $(win.system.computer): encoded command or hidden window (parent $(win.eventdata.parentImage)).
UC11 PowerShell download cradle on $(win.system.computer): web content executed directly in memory.
UC11 PowerShell download cradle found in a decoded script block on $(win.system.computer) (event 4104).

say.why: Almost every Windows intrusion uses PowerShell to hide its command or pull the next stage.
say.logic: Encoded or hidden PowerShell, and download cradles (download + Invoke-Expression) on the command line or in the decoded script block.
say.fp: SCCM and Intune are excluded by parent process; cradle rules need both the download and iex.
say.improve: PowerShell transcription to a protected share.

usecases.why_long: Almost every commodity intrusion on Windows runs PowerShell at some point: to hide its command line, to pull the next stage from the internet, or to run it straight from memory. A staff PC in a pilgrim agency has no reason to run encoded, hidden PowerShell.
logic: 111101 (level 10): `-EncodedCommand` (any abbreviation, `-e` to `-encodedcommand`) with a base64 blob, or a hidden window.

111102 (level 12): a download cradle on the command line, i.e. a web download (`DownloadString`, `Invoke-WebRequest`, `iwr`, `irm`, `Start-BitsTransfer`...) and `Invoke-Expression`/`iex` in the same command.
111103 (level 12): the same cradle in the decoded script block (event 4104). This catches it even when the command line itself was encoded.
fp: SCCM (`CcmExec`) and Intune agents use `-EncodedCommand` legitimately; they are excluded by parent process (`negate="yes"`), not by a global allowlist.
The cradle rules need BOTH a download primitive and `iex`; either alone is common admin work (cases UC11-04/05).
improve: Turn on PowerShell transcription to a protected share for full session context.

say.why: Attackers use Microsoft's own tools so antivirus stays quiet.
say.logic: Abuse syntax of certutil, bitsadmin, regsvr32, rundll32; tools identified by the PE OriginalFileName so renaming does not hide them.
say.fp: certutil -dump / -hashfile stay quiet; our rules hang under Wazuh's 92075/92018 so one event gives one alert.
say.improve: Correlate the download with a process started from the downloaded path.

usecases.why_long: Attackers avoid bringing tools that antivirus knows; they use the ones Microsoft ships (certutil, bitsadmin, regsvr32, rundll32) to fetch and unpack the next stage. In an agency network these tools have almost no daily business use, so their abuse syntax is a strong signal.
logic: 111201: certutil `-urlcache` / `-verifyctl` with a URL, any file type. Wazuh's 92075 only knows .exe/.dll.
111202: certutil `-decode` / `-decodehex`, any output. Wazuh's 92018 only knows output to .exe.
111203: bitsadmin `/transfer`, `/addfile`, `/download`.  111204: regsvr32 loading a remote scriptlet (Squiblydoo).  111205: rundll32 running JavaScript or a URL.
111206: one of these tools (or PowerShell) running under another file name. Tools are matched by `OriginalFileName` from the PE header, so renaming certutil.exe does not hide it.
111201/111202/111206 are also children of Wazuh's 92075, 92018, 92016, 92017 and 92051. Whichever rule the event reaches first, the final alert is the UC12 one.
fp: Each rule targets abuse syntax, not the tool: `certutil -dump` or `certutil -hashfile` stay quiet (cases UC12-09/10).
Software that ships a renamed copy of a Microsoft tool is extremely rare; allowlist it by path if it appears.
improve: Correlate a LOLBin download with a new process started from the downloaded path within 5 minutes.
Add Sysmon event 3 (network connection) for these tools to see the destination IP.

rules.description: UC17 sudo configuration changed on the web server: $(file)

say.why: A web shell runs as www-data; the next step is root, through sudoers or sudo.
say.logic: FIM with report_changes reads the diff: an ADDED non-comment line with NOPASSWD or ALL=(ALL) ALL is level 13; sudo by a service account after a web-shell signal is 14-15.
say.fp: Comment lines and removals stay low; admins using sudo keep Wazuh's normal levels.
say.improve: FIM whodata to show which process and user made the change.

usecases.why_long: web01 serves the booking portal. An attacker who gets a web shell runs as `www-data`; the next step is root, either by planting a sudoers rule or by abusing sudo. Root on web01 means the whole pilgrim database and the ability to tamper with bookings.
logic: 111701 (10): `/etc/sudoers` or a drop-in under `/etc/sudoers.d` was modified or deleted.  111702 (12): a new drop-in appeared.
111703 (13): the change ADDS a rule with `NOPASSWD`, `!authenticate` or full `ALL=(ALL) ALL`. The rule reads the line diff that `report_changes` attaches to the FIM event and ignores comment lines.
111704 (12): a web service account (`etc/lists/pp-service-accounts`) ran sudo. The list lookup on `user` checks the caller (srcuser), not the target.
111705 (15) / 111706 (14): the sudo attempt came within 30 minutes of a script being planted in the web root (UC07 110701) or of the web account running unexpected programs (UC07 110702).
Wazuh will not reuse an event that already triggered a correlation of the same or higher level, so these chains key on 110701/110702 rather than on UC07's level-15 110703.
fp: Only ADDED, non-comment lines are read: removing rights or adding a comment stays at 111701 (case UC17-05).
Administrators using sudo keep Wazuh's normal levels (case UC17-09).
improve: Turn on FIM `whodata` for these paths to show which process and login user made the change.
Active response: lock the service account's shell when 111705 fires.

111902 (12): a Defender exclusion was added (5007). 111903 (13): the exclusion is a whole drive, a user-writable folder, an executable or script extension, or a script host.

111904 (12): Tamper Protection blocked a change that would weaken Defender (5013 with a Disable* value going to 1, or an exclusion); found live: switching protection back on logs 5013 `0 -> 0`, which no longer alerts.  111905 (12): command lines that add exclusions, set Defender `Disable*` policy values or stop its services.  111906 (13): Wazuh's own Set-MpPreference rules re-raised in this use case.

say.why: Stolen Windows credentials turn one infected PC into access to every system that user has.
say.logic: LSASS opened with memory-read rights (access bits, not fixed masks), dump routines in the call stack, comsvcs MiniDump, SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive export.
say.fp: Windows and security processes that legitimately read LSASS are excluded by path; query-only access does not match.
say.improve: Turn on LSA protection and Credential Guard and alert if they are disabled.

usecases.why_long: Stolen Windows credentials turn one infected staff PC into access to every system the staff member uses, including the booking back office and the document share. Dumping LSASS or the SAM hive is the standard way to get them.
logic: 112001 (12): a process opened lsass.exe with rights that allow reading its memory or duplicating its handles. The rule reads the access BITS (`PROCESS_VM_READ` 0x10, `PROCESS_DUP_HANDLE` 0x40) instead of a few fixed masks, so 0x1410, 0x1438, 0x1fffff are caught; Wazuh's 92900 only knows 0x1010 and 0x40.
112002 (14): ...and the call stack shows a dump routine (dbghelp/dbgcore `MiniDumpWriteDump`, comsvcs.dll) or code with no backing module.
112003 (14): rundll32 calling comsvcs.dll MiniDump.  112004 (14): reg.exe saving or exporting the SAM, SECURITY or SYSTEM hive (Wazuh's 92026 only knows SAM).
fp: Windows and security processes that legitimately read LSASS (csrss, wininit, services, lsm, svchost, WMI, Program Files, the Defender platform folder) are excluded by path (case UC20-07).
Query-only access (0x1000) does not match (case UC20-08); exporting a single key under HKLM\SYSTEM does not match (UC20-09).
improve: Turn on LSA protection (RunAsPPL) and Credential Guard, and alert if they are switched off.

usecases.why_long: After the first foothold an intruder asks the machine who am I, where am I and who is admin, by running a quick series of built-in commands. Each one is normal for IT; five different ones in two minutes from one user is a person exploring.
logic: 112101/112102/112103 classify discovery tools, read-only `net` verbs and `wmic`/`netsh ... show` at level 4 with `no_log`. Level 4 is needed because Wazuh's net.exe rules are level 3 and would claim the event first; `no_log` keeps them off the dashboard while they are still stored for correlation.

112109 is a funnel: every classified command passes through this one rule so it is stored exactly once. A rule with several parents sits in several places in Wazuh's rule tree, and group correlation stores the event once per place, so a 5-event threshold could fire after 2 events (found and fixed in the engine).
112110 (10): 5 commands, of different tools (`different_field originalFileName`), by the same user within 2 minutes.
112111 (13): the burst happens on a host that raised a phishing, PowerShell or LOLBin alert (UC10-UC12) in the last 30 min.
112104 (8): domain-level discovery (`nltest /domain_trusts`, `net group "domain admins" /domain`) alerts on its own.
fp: A single command, or the same tool five times, stays silent (cases UC21-02, UC21-04).
Inventory launched by SCCM or Intune is excluded by parent process (case UC21-07).

Found live in the lab: the Wazuh agent's own SCA scan runs `net user` and `wmic useraccount ... get` as SYSTEM at every agent start, which fired 112110. The agent (`ossec-agent\wazuh-agent.exe`) is now excluded as a parent (case UC21-08).
`net.exe` starts `net1.exe` with the same arguments; the child is not counted again, so repeated net commands never look like two different tools (case UC21-09).
`net user ... /add` is left to Wazuh's own net.exe rules (case UC21-05) and to UC15.
improve: Add PowerShell discovery cmdlets from script block logging (`Get-LocalGroupMember`, `Get-ADUser`).
Raise to level 13 when the burst runs under a remote session (logon type 3 or 10).

decoders.pp-pilgrim_portal_decoders.xml:
<!--
  Pilgrim Services Portal - custom decoder
  Log source : /var/log/pilgrim-portal/portal.log  (web01, Wazuh agent, log_format=syslog)

  Each line has a syslog header followed by a JSON body:
    Nov 10 20:15:03 web01 pilgrim-portal[812]: {"event":"login_failed","srcip":"203.0.113.9","username":"pilgrim0042",...}

  How it works
    1. Wazuh's pre-decoder reads the syslog header and sets program_name = "pilgrim-portal".
    2. The parent decoder claims every event whose program_name is exactly pilgrim-portal.
       Because it keys on program_name, the built-in generic "json" decoder never sees these lines.
    3. The child decoder hands the JSON body to Wazuh's JSON plugin, so every key becomes a field
       usable in rules: event, username, role, country, result, pilgrim_id, record_count ...
       The key "srcip" lands in Wazuh's static source-IP field, which is what same_srcip,
       CDB address lookups and active response all rely on.

  Verified with the Wazuh 4.14.9 rule engine (wazuh-logtest).
-->

<decoder name="pilgrim-portal">
  <program_name>^pilgrim-portal$</program_name>
</decoder>

<decoder name="pilgrim-portal-fields">
  <parent>pilgrim-portal</parent>
  <plugin_decoder>JSON_Decoder</plugin_decoder>
</decoder>
